title: The group axioms
objectives: Check the group axioms and prove that identities and inverses are unique.

screens.title: Four checks
screens.prose: Here are four sets with an operation, and four checks on each. One cell is still open: is subtraction associative? Brackets decide what is done first.
screens.question: $(5 - 3) - 1 = 1$. Work out $5 - (3 - 1)$.

hints.text: Work out the bracket first.
$5 - 2 = 3$, which is not 1.

feedback.correct: Right: 3, not 1. Subtraction is not associative.
feedback.generic: Not quite. Do $3 - 1$ first, then take it from 5.

byKey.same: You got 1 again, as if the brackets did not matter. Work out 3 − 1 = 2 first, then 5 − 2.

explain.text: $5 - (3 - 1) = 5 - 2 = 3$ but $(5 - 3) - 1 = 1$. One failed triple is enough: subtraction is not associative.

screens.title: Which pass every check
screens.prose: A set with an operation that passes all four checks is a **group** (Pinter chapter 3). The checks are the group axioms: closure, associativity, an identity, and an inverse for every element.
screens.question: Tap every row that is a group.

hints.text: A group needs yes in all four columns.
$(\mathbb{Z}, \times)$ fails one check: what is the inverse of 2?
Only $(\mathbb{Z}, +)$ and $(\mathbb{Q} \setminus \{0\}, \times)$ pass all four.

feedback.generic: Not quite. Keep only rows with yes in every column.

byKey.r2: You kept $(\mathbb{Z}, \times)$. No integer $x$ has $2x = 1$, so 2 has no inverse.
byKey.r1: You kept subtraction. It fails associativity, as the first screen showed.

explain.text: Integers under addition and non-zero rationals under multiplication pass all four checks. Subtraction fails associativity, and $(\mathbb{Z}, \times)$ has no inverse for 2.

screens.title: Positive reals
screens.prose: Take the positive reals $\mathbb{R}_{>0}$ under multiplication. Run the four checks on a few numbers first.
screens.question: Which is the first axiom that fails, if any?

options.why: You looked for a whole-number inverse. The inverse 1/x is a positive real, so it is in the set.
You worried a product might leave the set. A product of two positive numbers is positive.

hints.text: Check each axiom against the table.
For inverses, is $1/x$ positive when $x$ is?
All four hold, so it is a group.

feedback.generic: Not quite. Test each axiom in turn.

explain.text: Products of positive reals are positive, multiplication is associative, 1 is the identity and $1/x$ is the inverse. All four axioms hold.

screens.title: All 2 by 2 matrices
screens.prose: Now take every real $2 \times 2$ matrix under matrix multiplication. The identity is $\mathbf{I}$. Look at $\mathbf{A} = \begin{pmatrix}1&2\\2&4\end{pmatrix}$.
screens.question: Which is the first axiom that fails, if any?

options.why: You doubted closure. Two 2 by 2 matrices always multiply to a 2 by 2 matrix.
You doubted associativity. Matrix multiplication is associative, as composing maps is.
You missed the singular matrix. A matrix with determinant 0 has no inverse.

hints.text: Which matrices have no inverse?
$\det \mathbf{A} = 0$.
A matrix with determinant 0 cannot be undone, so inverses fail.

feedback.correct: Right. Inverses fail, so we keep only the invertible matrices.
feedback.generic: Not quite. Look at the determinant of $\mathbf{A}$.

explain.text: $\det \mathbf{A} = 0$, so $\mathbf{A}$ has no inverse and the axioms fail. The invertible $2 \times 2$ matrices do form a group. It is not **abelian**: there $\mathbf{AB} \ne \mathbf{BA}$ in general, as in `vectors` l7.

screens.title: Multiplying modulo 5
screens.prose: Take $\{0, 1, 2, 3, 4\}$ under multiplication modulo 5: multiply, then keep the remainder on division by 5.
screens.question: Which is the first axiom that fails, if any?

options.why: You thought 12 leaves the set. We keep the remainder, so every product lands in 0 to 4.
You missed the identity. 1 times anything is that thing.

hints.text: Look for an element nothing can undo.
What is 0 times any number, modulo 5?
0 has no inverse. Remove it and $\{1, 2, 3, 4\}$ passes.

feedback.generic: Not quite. Try to undo multiplication by 0.

explain.text: 0 times anything is 0, so 0 has no inverse. Drop it: in $\{1, 2, 3, 4\}$ the inverses are $1, 3, 2, 4$, so that set is a group.

screens.title: One inverse only
screens.prose: We write $a^{-1}$ for the inverse of $a$. That name needs proof that there is only one. Suppose $ab = ba = e$ and $ac = ca = e$.
screens.question: Order the chain that proves $b = c$. Leave out the line that does not belong.

lines.text: $ec = c$, since $e$ is the identity. So $b = c$.

lines.why: You wrote $a^{-1}$, but that name already assumes $a$ has only one inverse. That is what we are proving.

hints.text: Start from $b$ and slip in $e = ac$.
Each line uses one axiom or one hypothesis.
$b = be = b(ac) = (ba)c = ec = c$.

feedback.correct: That is the proof: $b = be = b(ac) = (ba)c = ec = c$.
feedback.generic: Not quite. Each line changes one thing, by one reason.

byKey.left-out: You left out a step. The chain needs all five links.

explain.text: We wrote $e$ as $ac$, regrouped, and replaced $ba$ by $e$. Every step used an axiom or a hypothesis, so the two inverses agree.

screens.title: Cancelling
screens.prose: In a group, $ab = ac$ forces $b = c$. Put the steps in order. The $D_4$ table from l1 is below: no row repeats an element.
screens.question: Order the cancellation proof. Leave out the false step.

lines.text: $a^{-1}(ab) = a^{-1}(ac)$: multiply both sides on the left by $a^{-1}$.

lines.why: You divided, but a group has no division. We may only multiply by $a^{-1}$, on the left here.

hints.text: What undoes $a$ on the left?
Multiply both sides by $a^{-1}$ on the left, then regroup.
Given, multiply, regroup, replace, identity.

feedback.correct: Right. So two cells of one row never hold the same element.
feedback.generic: Not quite. Multiply by the inverse first, then regroup.

byKey.left-out: You left out a step the proof needs.

explain.text: Multiplying by $a^{-1}$ on the left and regrouping turns $ab = ac$ into $b = c$. So row $a$ of a Cayley table holds each element once: in row $r$ of $D_4$ all eight appear.

screens.title: Undoing a product
screens.prose: In $D_4$ take $a = r$ and $b = s$, so $ab = rs$. We want the move that undoes $rs$.

state.caption: The square after rs: flip, then turn.

screens.question: Which element is $(rs)^{-1}$?

options.why: You undid $r$ first. But $r$ was done last, so it must be undone first. Doing $r^3s$ after $rs$ gives the half turn $r^2$, not $e$.

canvas.caption: rs, then r³s: a half turn, not home.

options.why: You undid the turn only. The flip still has to be undone.

hints.text: Socks and shoes: what goes on last comes off first.
$rs$ does $s$, then $r$. Undo $r$, then undo $s$.
Undo $r$ with $r^3$, then $s$ with $s$: that is $s \cdot r^3$, which the table gives as $rs$.

feedback.correct: Right. $rs$ is a flip, so it undoes itself, and $s^{-1}r^{-1}$ agrees.
feedback.generic: Not quite. Undo the last move first.

byKey.same: You inverted each factor but kept the order. The inverse of $ab$ is $b^{-1}a^{-1}$, not $a^{-1}b^{-1}$.

explain.text: The inverse of $ab$ is $b^{-1}a^{-1}$: shoes off before socks. Here $s^{-1}r^{-1} = sr^3 = rs$, a flip that undoes itself. But $r^{-1}s^{-1} = r^3s$ is a different flip.

screens.title: Shoes before socks
screens.prose: Now prove $(ab)^{-1} = b^{-1}a^{-1}$ in any group. It is enough to multiply and reach $e$, since inverses are unique.
screens.question: Order the check. Leave out the flawed line.

lines.text: $aea^{-1} = aa^{-1} = e$, since $e$ is the identity and $aa^{-1} = e$.
The product the other way is $e$ too, so $b^{-1}a^{-1}$ is the inverse of $ab$.

lines.why: You moved $b$ past $a^{-1}$. That needs $ba^{-1} = a^{-1}b$, which fails in $D_4$.

hints.text: Multiply $ab$ by $b^{-1}a^{-1}$ and regroup.
The two middle letters $bb^{-1}$ meet first.
Regroup, cancel the middle, cancel the outside, conclude.

feedback.correct: That is the proof. Uniqueness from the last screens does the rest.
feedback.generic: Not quite. Regroup so that $b$ meets $b^{-1}$ first.

byKey.left-out: You left out a step the proof needs.

explain.text: Regrouping brings $b$ next to $b^{-1}$, then $a$ next to $a^{-1}$. Both products give $e$, and inverses are unique, so $(ab)^{-1} = b^{-1}a^{-1}$.

screens.title: Compounding returns
screens.prose: Returns combine by $r_1 \oplus r_2 = (1 + r_1)(1 + r_2) - 1$: growth factors multiply, as in `exp-log` l6. A fund gains $10\%$ in May and loses $10\%$ in June.
screens.question: What is the combined return $10\% \oplus (-10\%)$?

hints.text: Multiply the growth factors, then subtract 1.

feedback.correct: Right: $-1\%$. The loss is applied to a bigger balance.
feedback.generic: Not quite. Multiply the factors 1.10 and 0.90, then subtract 1.

byKey.zero: You added the returns: 10% − 10% = 0. Returns compound: the factors multiply to 0.99.

screens.title: Undoing a loss
screens.prose: The inverse of a return $r$ is the return that brings the factor back to 1: $(1 + r)(1 + r') = 1$, so $r' = -\tfrac{r}{1 + r}$. A portfolio loses $20\%$.
screens.question: What return undoes a $20\%$ loss?

hints.text: Find the factor that multiplies 0.80 back to 1.
A factor of 1.25 is a gain of 25%.

byKey.same: You undid $-20\%$ with $+20\%$. That gives $0.80 \times 1.20 = 0.96$, still 4% down.

explain.text: $r' = -\tfrac{-0.2}{0.8} = 0.25$, a $25\%$ gain. Inverses exist only for $r > -100\%$, so the group is returns above $-100\%$ under $\oplus$.

screens.title: Checking by brute force
screens.prose: Write `is_group(elements, op)`. It returns `True` when `op` is closed and associative on the list, with an identity and inverses. Try every pair and triple. `D4` and `compose` are defined for you. Passing every case is a proof for that finite group only.
screens.question: Finish is_group so that all four axioms are checked.

examples.call: is_group([1, 2, 3, 4, 5], lambda a, b: a * b % 6)

tests.name: mul5-zero
tests.call: is_group(list(range(5)), lambda a, b: a * b % 5)

tests.name: mul5
tests.call: is_group([1, 2, 3, 4], lambda a, b: a * b % 5)

tests.name: mul6
tests.call: is_group([1, 2, 3, 4, 5], lambda a, b: a * b % 6)

widget.how: The first Check starts Python, which takes a few seconds. Submit runs 8 hidden tests; each must equal the expected value exactly.

hints.text: The starter checks closure only. Add the other three checks.
Associativity: compare op(op(a, b), c) with op(a, op(b, c)) for every triple.
Find e with op(e, x) == x == op(x, e) for all x, then look for each inverse.

feedback.correct: All eight cases pass. Multiplication modulo 5 fails only because of 0.
feedback.generic: Not yet. Check the failing rows: which axiom does that case break?

explain.text: Subtraction modulo 5 is closed but not associative, and 0 has no inverse under multiplication. A finite check over every pair and triple settles each case.

ideas: A group is a set with an operation that is closed and associative. It has an identity, and each element has an inverse.
The identity is unique, and so is each inverse: $b = be = b(ac) = (ba)c = ec = c$.
Cancellation holds, so each row of a Cayley table holds every element once.

quiz.question: Suppose $e$ and $e'$ are both identities. Order the proof that $e = e'$.

feedback.generic: Not quite. Use $e'$ as the identity first, then $e$.

explain.text: Read $ee'$ two ways. As $e$ times an identity it is $e$; as an identity times $e'$ it is $e'$.

quiz.question: Cancellation says $ab = ac$ forces $b = c$. What does that tell us about a Cayley table?

options.text: Each element appears exactly once in each row.
The table is symmetric about its diagonal.
options.why: You described an abelian group's table. $D_4$'s is not symmetric, since $rs \ne sr$.

options.text: The diagonal holds only the identity.
options.why: You assumed every element undoes itself. In $D_4$, $r \cdot r = r^2$.

feedback.correct: Right. Two equal cells in row a would mean ab = ac with b ≠ c.
feedback.generic: Not quite. Think of row a, which holds ab for every b.

explain.text: Row $a$ holds $ab$ for each column $b$. If two cells agreed, cancellation would make their columns equal. So no element repeats in a row.

quiz.question: Why do we take the group of returns to be the returns above $-100\%$?

options.text: A $-100\%$ return leaves nothing, so no later return can undo it.

options.why: You applied $-r/(1 + r)$ at $r = -1$. It divides by zero, so there is no inverse at all.
$0\%$ is the identity, and it undoes itself.

feedback.correct: Right. The factor $1 + r$ is 0, and nothing times 0 is 1.
feedback.generic: Not quite. Look at the growth factor of a −100% return.

explain.text: A $-100\%$ return has growth factor $0$. No factor multiplies 0 back to 1, so it has no inverse.

quiz.question: The table below has identity $e$ and $a \cdot b = e$. Why can it not be a group table?

options.text: Row $b$ holds $b$ twice, so $ba = be$ with $a \ne e$.
It has 3 elements, and a group needs an even number.
options.why: You ruled out odd sizes. $\{0, 1, 2\}$ under addition modulo 3 is a group of 3.
Row $e$ and column $e$ copy the heads, so $e$ is an identity.

feedback.generic: Not quite. Look for a row that repeats an element.

explain.text: $ba = b = be$, so cancelling $b$ would give $a = e$. Also $ab = e$ but $ba \ne e$. A true table on $\{e, a, b\}$ with $ab = e$ has row $b$ equal to $b, e, a$.
